sweep_summary: Two title-works with stress in the title: Downing 2004 (ZASPiL 37, open at zaspil.leibniz-zas.de, downloaded/read) reports Tucker 1994 p. 18 — Dholuo stress on the stem-initial vowel, morphologically determined, unmoved by affixes — which confirms the catalog's 'morphological' coding; Schiller 1982 is a history dissertation on two Luo polities 'under stress' (Glottolog/EBALL record only), not relevant. From files already held by the project I also read Oduor 2002 (UoN PhD, first-hand): a weight-based account — stress on the last heavy syllable, penultimate in V-final and final in C-final words utterance-finally, diagnosed by vowel doubling; her review reports Omondi 1982 (root-syllable stress), Stafford 1967 and Odhiambo 1981 (penultimate). Blount 1969 (after Gregersen 1961:40) says regular penultimate stress. Best first-hand statement read: Oduor 2002 p. 163; it refines/competes with but does not supersede Cable 2009/Tucker 1994. Nothing left unread that needs acquiring from the item list; Tucker 1994 itself and Nimura 1996 (UoN thesis, no open file) remain the unobtained primary sources. Glottolog and Crossref were queried by automated download instead.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Dholuo is detected towards the end of an utterance, through vowel doubling. Stress therefore has the effect of doubling Dholuo vowels. In a vowel final word stress is detected on the penultimate syllable and in a consonant final word, stress is detected on the last syllable. This stress pattern is what Okombo (1982) calls root lengthening (see section 1.7.2.2.4 above). [...] The discussions of stress in Dholuo words, in sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3, also show that stress is on the penultimate syllable in words ending in a vowel and on the last syllable in words ending in a consonant.
new_statements.citation: Oduor, Jane Akinyi Ngala. 2002. A study of syllable weight and its effects in Dholuo phonology. PhD thesis, University of Nairobi (hdl 11295/18409)
new_statements.reading: The only first-hand primary source read this search of works with stress in the title. Oduor (native-speaker linguist, KSN dialect) analyses Dholuo stress as quantity-sensitive: primary stress on the last heavy syllable, surfacing as penultimate in vowel-final and final in consonant-final words when utterance-final, cued by vowel doubling (= Okombo's root-lengthening). Her data are largely reconcilable with the catalog's root-initial (morphological) account — prefixed a-par/a-dek are stressed on the root, most disyllables initially — but her stated generalisation is positional/weight-based, not morphological, and her heaviness criterion is partly the stress cue itself. Downing 2004 (pp. 109-110, reporting Tucker 1994 p. 18: stress on the stem-initial vowel, morphologically determined, immobile under affixation) directly confirms the catalog's 'morphological' coding; Blount 1969 (after Gregersen 1961:40) and Stafford 1967 (via Oduor p. 68) give 'penultimate'. Net: the catalog's classification stands, with Oduor 2002 and the Gregersen/Stafford line worth recording as competing positional analyses.

new_statements.quote: I. In words ending with a vowel the accent is on the penultima. This accent remains on that syllable notwithstanding the addition of other syllables. Pála: knife. Pélinigo: those knives. II. In words ending in a consonant the accent falls on the last syllable. Manyakachieng': eternal. III. For emphasis' sake some vowels are drawn out to a considerable length. A-a-a-a-a-uchiel: six. Cho-o-o-o-n: formerly, early.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's morphological (stem-anchored, immobile under affixation) coding: the Handbook explicitly says the accent 'remains on that syllable notwithstanding the addition of other syllables'. Its stated surface rule (penultimate in vowel-final words, final in consonant-final words) is word for word the generalisation Oduor 2002 gives on p. 163, and it is the source-type behind the Gregersen 1961 / Stafford 1967 'penultimate' line already noted in existing_statements. It adds the possessive-singular vs plural accent contrast and the future/past sentence-accent note, neither of which the catalog records.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For a bare word, accent is on the penultimate syllable if the word ends in a vowel and on the last syllable if it ends in a consonant; but the accent stays on that same (stem) syllable when further syllables are suffixed (Pála 'knife' > Pélinigo 'those knives'), so the accent is anchored to the stem rather than counted from the right edge. Read as stem-anchored (morphological) stress whose surface position in unsuffixed words is penult (V-final) or final (C-final).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. Emphatic vowel lengthening (item III) is described as expressive, not as a second degree of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 17, Remark II: when the possessive (construct) form of the singular is segmentally identical to the plural, 'the accent falls on the last syllable, whereas in the plural it falls on the penultimate, e.g., Aguch Maria — Mary's cooking-pot (but aguch Maria — Mary's cooking pots)'. pp. 55-56: in passive sentences 'In the future the accent falls on the verb, Pipanoom — The barrel will be downloaded. In the Past Tense it falls on the tense prefix: Pipi noom — The barrel was downloaded' (sentence-level accent distinguishing tenses). 'Accent' is never defined; tone is not mentioned anywhere in the grammar, so some of these 'accent' contrasts may be tonal.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1921 Handbook calls the language 'Kavirondo' (also 'Nilotic' in its chapter headings), i.e. the Nilotic Luo of the Kisumu / Kavirondo Gulf area of Kenya, which is Dholuo; the archive.org description calls it one of the earliest written accounts of Dholuo. Owino 2003 describes Kenyan Dholuo without naming a dialect in the pages read. Okombo 1982 is a general Dholuo phonology. The archive.org 'Kavirondo' item is Part 1 only (grammar and phraseology).

new_statements.quote: Stress in Dholuo falls mainly on the stem vowel of a word and never on the affix, except in the plural forms of verbs in the imperative, where stress may fall on the suffix (Tucker & Bryan 1966). This can be seen in the following examples: 18). Dholuo English nìndí sleep (imperative) kàdhí pass (imperative). Stress in Dholuo is normally accompanied by length, although length is not distinctive. The addition of prefixes and suffixes does not upset the pattern between stress and length, which is a fundamental difference from the case of Swahili. In the latter, stress will always shift to the penultimate syllable. [p. 64:] As in many other African languages, tone plays an important role in Dholuo. [p. 79:] In a tone language like Dholuo, a word may have more than one high tone, but a stress language can only have one stressed syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's morphological coding and as Downing 2004 / Tucker 1994 in existing_statements: stress on the stem vowel, immobile under affixation. Adds the imperative-plural suffix exception, the statement that length is the (non-distinctive) correlate of stress, and an explicit statement that Dholuo is a tone language (which the catalog record does not mention).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the stem (root) vowel, never on an affix, and does not move when prefixes or suffixes are added; it is cued by non-distinctive vowel length. Dholuo is at the same time a tone language with lexical and grammatical tone (sec. 2.8). The one exception given is the plural imperative of verbs, where stress may fall on the suffix.
new_statements.exceptions: Plural imperative verbs, where stress may fall on the suffix (nìndí 'sleep', kàdhí 'pass'; note the examples are marked with tone diacritics, not stress marks). p. 55 (after Tucker 1994:29): epenthetic vowels are never stressed in speech though they carry a tone, but in Luo music they may be given full vocalic value and even stressed. The stress statement is second-hand from Tucker & Bryan 1966; chapter 5 (pp. 164-175) concerns how English and Swahili stress is rendered as high tone / falling tone and as ATR harmony in loanwords, not native stress placement.

readall_conflicts: No opened source contradicts the catalog's morphological (stem-anchored) coding, but the two describe it from different angles. The 1921 Handbook states a positional surface rule (penultimate in vowel-final words, final in consonant-final words) and then, in the same paragraph, says the accent stays on its syllable under suffixation (Pála > Pélinigo), so a purely positional/right-edge reading of the Handbook would be contradicted by its own example; its rule is the same generalisation Oduor 2002 (p. 163) and the Gregersen/Stafford 'penultimate' line give for bare words. Owino 2003 (after Tucker & Bryan 1966) states stress on the stem vowel, never on affixes, immobile under affixation, which agrees with Downing 2004 / Tucker 1994 in the existing statements. Two smaller discrepancies: Owino records an exception (plural imperative stresses the suffix) that no other source mentions, and the Handbook's possessive-singular vs plural 'accent' contrast (aguch Maria) and its future/past sentence-accent note are undefined 'accent' phenomena in a book that never mentions tone, so they may be tonal rather than stress contrasts. Okombo 1982 and Scruggs 1980 could not be opened.

audit.recode_to: Likely phonological, quantity-sensitive, right-edge: main stress on the last heavy (VV / lengthened) syllable = penult in vowel-final words, final in consonant-final words, initial default in all-light words (Okoth-Okombo 1982; Oduor 2002 ch. 4, 2015b, 2017); drop the Cable-only 'trochaic L-to-R alternating secondary stress' the secondary-stress rule (no primary source states it). Keep a note that Tucker 1994 / the 1921 handbook describe the same facts as root-anchored (accent stays under encliticization), so final third reading of morphological vs phonological should be made with Tucker 1994's stress section in hand; at minimum re-read with Oduor 2002 and add it as a contra source.

sources.note: First-hand metrical (weight-based) analysis, KSN dialect: primary stress on the last heavy syllable; diagnosed by utterance-final vowel doubling, so it lands on the penult in V-final words and the final in C-final words (= Okombo's 'root-lengthening'); most disyllables (incl. verbs tedo) stressed initially, but prefixed a-par 'ten', a-dek 'three' stressed on the second (root) syllable; plural-imperative suffix -uru stressed on its first syllable. Also reports the earlier literature: Omondi 1982 (fixed root-syllable stress), Stafford 1967 (penultimate, immobile under suffixation, except -uru),…

Suprasegmentals: a. stress: falls regularly on the penultimate syllable with secondary stress on geminate vowels (Gregersen 40), b. tone: (1) high tone does not occur in an unaccented syllable except after midtone. sources.note: Second-hand summary of Gregersen 1961 (Luo: a grammar), p. 40: regular penultimate stress, secondary stress on geminate vowels; tone restrictions keyed to stressed penult/ultima. A positional (penultimate) statement, at odds with the root-initial account but consistent with the CVCV canon where root = penult.

sources.quote: However, Dholuo (E. Nilotic) is described by Tucker (1993) as having stress as well as tone. Stress is assigned to the stem-initial vowel. (That is, stress placement is determined by morphological, not phonological, position.) When a word is in phrase-final position, the stressed vowel is noticeably lengthened, at least in some dialects. [...] Since stress is morphologically determined, words of identical lengths but different morphological structures will be stressed on different syllables, as shown in (6a). And adding suffixes does not change the position of stress away from the stem vowel, as shown in (6b). (6) Dholuo stress (Tucker 1993, p 18) [...] (a) ra+hî 'cobra' vs rawo 'hippo' (b) ra+hí+nì 'this cobra' vs. rawo+ni 'this hippo'
sources.note: Survey chapter (second-hand, reporting Tucker 1993/1994 p. 18): Dholuo has stress plus tone; stress is fixed on the stem-initial vowel, i.e. morphologically determined, unaffected by prefixes or suffixes; the stressed vowel is lengthened phrase-finally in some dialects. Groups Dholuo with Lango, Dinka, Shilluk as Nilotic 'morphemic stress' languages.
